body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Real-time feedback from electronic hand hygiene monitoring on medical wards: a cluster randomised trial","authors":"Okafor-Lindahl S, Brennan-Tshabalala M, Iwata-Moreau J","year":2022,"venue":"Wrenmouth Hospital Infection Research","doi":"10.5555/hicr.2022.0187","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Methods: twelve medical wards with badge-based hand hygiene monitoring were randomised to real-time vibration feedback with weekly ward dashboards or to silent monitoring for six months. The primary outcome was compliance recorded by the electronic system at patient-zone entry. Results: electronic compliance rose from 48 to 71 percent on feedback wards and from 50 to 54 percent on control wards (difference in change 19 percentage points, 95 percent CI 11 to 27). Directly observed compliance, a secondary outcome measured on a random sample of shifts, was 64 against 57 percent. Healthcare-associated infections were too few for comparison. Conclusions: real-time feedback increased hand hygiene compliance."},{"title":"Visible observers and dispenser activity on four wards: observed hand hygiene compared with concurrent covert counts","authors":"Stavros-Mbeki A, Lund-Oyeyemi T","year":2019,"venue":"Infection Prevention Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On four wards we compared hand hygiene events counted covertly by dispenser sensors during hours when a trained observer was visibly present with the same hours on days without an observer. Dispenser events per hour were about three times higher when an observer was present, and the increase was confined to the area within the observer's line of sight. Compliance recorded by the observer was 78 percent, whereas covert counts implied a much lower rate. The effect did not fade over eight weeks of observation. Observer-based compliance therefore measures behaviour under observation rather than usual behaviour, and comparisons between groups are fair only if observation is equally visible in both."},{"title":"Badge and dispenser-based hand hygiene monitoring: a review of 31 evaluations of detection accuracy and feedback","authors":"Harrow-Delacroix P, Nwosu-Ekberg L, Tanaka-Fitzgerald R","year":2020,"venue":"Infection Prevention Reviews and Methods","doi":"10.5555/iprm.2020.0342","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 31 studies of electronic or automated hand hygiene monitoring systems. Accuracy against direct observation varied widely: badge systems detected between 53 and 91 percent of observed hand hygiene opportunities, and most missed opportunities during continuous care within a patient zone. Fourteen studies reported compliance after feedback was introduced; twelve reported improvement, but only two were randomised and most used the monitoring system's own measure as the outcome. No study showed a reduction in infections with adequate power. We recommend an outcome measured independently of the feedback system in any comparative evaluation."},{"title":"Badge-based hand hygiene monitoring and nurse acceptability on two surgical wards","authors":"Quinlan-Asante M, Borg-Adeyemi K","year":2017,"venue":"Nursing Workplace Perspectives","doi":"10.5555/nwp.2017.0091","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked nurses on two surgical wards about badge-based monitoring six months after it was introduced, using group discussions with 22 nurses and a short questionnaire returned by 61 of 94 nursing staff. Most accepted ward-level feedback but objected strongly to managers seeing individual data. Several nurses described touching a dispenser near the door to stop the badge vibrating during busy periods, without cleaning their hands. Night staff said vibration alerts woke patients in shared bays. Nurses asked for the rules on data use to be written down and agreed with staff representatives before any expansion of the system."},{"title":"Healthcare-associated infection rates after hand hygiene feedback dashboards: an interrupted time series in a regional hospital","authors":"Castellano-Obi R, Fenwick-Adjei D","year":2023,"venue":"Wrenmouth Hospital Infection Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined monthly counts of MRSA acquisition and hospital-onset C. difficile infection over 24 months before and 18 months after ward hand hygiene dashboards were introduced in a 480-bed hospital. Events averaged 3.1 per month across the hospital. There was no clear change in level or slope after the dashboards, and the confidence intervals were compatible with anything from a 30 percent reduction to a 20 percent increase. Hand rub consumption rose by 12 percent. The authors conclude that infection outcomes are too infrequent in a single hospital to evaluate hand hygiene interventions over short periods."},{"title":"Intracluster correlation coefficients for hand hygiene compliance in ward-randomised studies","authors":"Mbatha-Ruiz K, Holmberg-Chukwu O","year":2021,"venue":"Tamsford Trials Methodology Notes","doi":"10.5555/ctmn.2021.0064","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We estimated intracluster correlation coefficients from the individual observation data of six ward-randomised and cluster-level studies of hand hygiene. For compliance measured by direct observation, the intracluster correlation ranged from 0.04 to 0.09, with a median of 0.06. Coefficients were larger for physicians than for nurses and larger when observation sessions were short. Baseline ward compliance explained a substantial share of between-ward variation, so adjusting for it reduced the required number of wards. We provide the coefficients and their confidence intervals for use in planning future trials."},{"title":"Contamination between wards in cluster trials of hand hygiene interventions: staff movement and shared equipment","authors":"Ferrante-Osei L, Kaur-Lindstrom B","year":2024,"venue":"Wrenmouth Hospital Infection Research","doi":"10.5555/hicr.2024.0012","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In a completed trial of ward-level hand hygiene feedback, 22 percent of nursing shifts on control wards were worked by staff who also worked on intervention wards during the trial. Compliance among these float staff on control wards rose during the trial, and the difference between arms was about a third smaller than among staff who worked on one ward only. Shared portable equipment and joint handovers also carried feedback messages between wards. The authors recommend randomising pairs of wards that share staff as one cluster and recording float status for every observed opportunity."},{"title":"Alcohol-based hand rub consumption as a proxy for hand hygiene compliance: agreement with direct observation on 30 wards","authors":"Delgado-Nkemelu J, Sato-Birkeland E","year":2016,"venue":"Infection Prevention Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared monthly alcohol-based hand rub consumption per 1,000 patient-days with directly observed compliance on 30 wards over one year. The correlation between consumption and observed compliance was weak (r equal to 0.31), and consumption rose with patient acuity and with the number of visitors independently of observed staff behaviour. Consumption was cheap to collect and complete for every ward-month, but pump dispensers refilled from bulk stock were recorded inconsistently on six wards. The authors suggest consumption as a context measure rather than as a substitute for observed compliance."}]}
